Not All Entities are Created Equal: A Dynamic Anonymization Framework for Privacy-Preserving Retrieval-Augmented Generation

Xinyuan Zhu ††thanks: equal contribution    Zekun Fei11footnotemark: 1    Enye Wang    Ruiqi He    Zheli Liu ††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Nankai University Email: {zhuxinyuan,feizekun,wangenye,heruiqi}@mail.nankai.edu.cn Email: liuzheli@nankai.edu.cn
Abstract

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) enhances the utility of Large Language Models (LLMs) by retrieving external documents. Since the knowledge databases in RAG are predominantly utilized via cloud services, private data in sensitive domains such as finance and healthcare faces the risk of personal information leakage. Thus, effectively anonymizing knowledge bases is crucial for privacy preservation. Existing studies equate the privacy risk of text to the linear superposition of the privacy risks of individual, isolated sensitive entities. The "one-size-fits-all" full processing of all sensitive entities severely degrades utility of LLM. To address this issue, we introduce a dynamic anonymization framework named TRIP-RAG. Based on context-aware entity quantification, this framework evaluates entities from the perspectives of marginal privacy risk, knowledge divergence, and topical relevance. It identifies highly sensitive entities while trading off utility, providing a feasible approach for variable-intensity privacy protection scenarios. Our theoretical analysis and experiments indicate that TRIP-RAG can effectively reduce context inference risks. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that, while maintaining privacy protection comparable to full anonymization, TRIP-RAG’s Recall@k decreases by less than 35% compared to the original data, and the generation quality improves by up to 56% over existing baselines.

1 Introduction

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (Lewis et al. (2020)) retrieves relevant information from external knowledge bases, enabling Large Language Models (LLMs) to generate responses based on both the retrieved documents and their internal training knowledge. This approach effectively addresses the timeliness limitations of LLMs and mitigates their hallucinations.

However, Retrieval-Augmented Generation is typically provided as a cloud service where the server is inherently untrusted. As illustrated in Figure  1, uploading documents from sensitive domains such as finance and healthcare in their raw form inherently leads to the leakage of private information; for instance, in medical disease diagnosis (Chen et al. (2025),Li et al. (2023)), the original data within knowledge databases may contain patients’ personal information, such as gender and age. Even assuming a trusted server is employed, numerous attack vectors can still trigger privacy breaches. For example, context-based prompt attacks (Qi et al. (2024)) can extract raw data from knowledge databases by crafting simple prompts. Consequently, while RAG enhances utility, it concurrently raises significant concerns regarding personal information leakage.

Recently, some studies have conducted preliminary explorations on protecting the privacy of texts in knowledge databases, which can be categorized into data synthesis approaches and perturbation approaches. Zeng et al. (2025) utilized data synthesis to perform adversarial LLM rewriting on the entire text of knowledge databases, while He et al. (2025) proposed a solution based on local differential privacy to perturb sensitive entities . However, these methods primarily focus on the privacy of the entities themselves, neglecting the privacy interplay between the sentences and the entities. As shown in Figure  1, they attempt to achieve semantic privacy protection of the text by perturbing or eliminating all entities entirely, thereby overlooking the required variability in privacy protection intensity and the differences among entities. In fact, for a single document lacking additional context, such a “one-size-fits-all” solution is excessive and severely degrades the quality of the LLM’s retrieval and generation.

To address the aforementioned issues and challenges, we propose TRIP-RAG, a novel dynamic anonymization framework tailored for massive texts within knowledge databases of RAG. As illustrated in Figure 1, we posit that textual privacy does not necessitate the absolute protection of all related entities. Instead, by selectively anonymizing a subset of entities, we can achieve semantic anonymity for the text, thereby maximizing utility while preserving privacy guarantees. To resolve the priority issue of entity selection in localized anonymization, we focus for the first time on context-aware entity quantification within RAG scenarios, evaluating entities through a three-dimensional manifold that encompasses marginal privacy risk, knowledge divergence, and topical relevance. Specifically, by utilizing a small number of annotated samples to train a language model-based privacy-aware surrogate function, we leverage the concept of differential analysis to achieve marginal privacy risk detection for massive entities. Based on the semantic clustering property of high-dimensional vector spaces (Mikolov et al. (2013)), we quantify the stability of an entity with respect to the overall knowledge structure of the text using the cosine similarity of the text before and after entity masking. Furthermore, drawing on the RAG framework’s reliance on vector distance for retrieval (Lewis et al. (2020)), we treat entities as proxy queries to quantify their topical relevance to a document by computing the L2L_{2} distance between their respective latent representations. Through the comprehensive ranking of these three scores and dynamic threshold control, we realize an anonymization framework with adjustable privacy protection strength that fully preserves utility. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach maintains substantial text utility while safeguarding privacy, validating the superiority of our method.

The main contributions of this paper are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a dynamic anonymization framework tailored for the massive text scenarios in RAG knowledge databases, uniquely integrating a multi-dimensional quantitative assessment of entity privacy, knowledge, and retrieval utility.

  • •

    We provide a trade-off method between privacy and utility for numerous downstream tasks in the field of text anonymization.

  • •

    Cross-dataset, multi-model experiments demonstrate that our scheme quantifies and balances privacy and utility, achieving a percentage increase in utility with almost no impact on privacy.

2 Related Works

2.1 RAG Technology and Attack Methods

Proposed by Lewis et al. (2020), Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) is a method designed to enhance the generative capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs). By representing massive document corpora as dense embeddings to facilitate efficient semantic retrieval, RAG effectively mitigates LLM hallucinations and bolsters response reliability. Furthermore, its flexible document storage enables rapid updates to the model’s accessible knowledge base without requiring retraining. These advantages have established RAG as the preferred approach for deploying LLMs in knowledge-intensive domains, demonstrating significant utility in highly hallucination-prone scenarios such as medical disease diagnosis(Liang et al. (2025)).

However, while RAG enhances utility, it concurrently introduces significant privacy concerns. The knowledge databases utilized in RAG are typically deployed as cloud services (e.g., AWS(Enevoldsen et al. (2025))), which predominantly rely on proprietary black-box embedding models to drive Vector Database (VDB) embedding services. This paradigm renders the server-side inherently untrustworthy. Since texts in sensitive domains frequently contain sensitive data, storing original documents naturally leads to the leakage of private information. Furthermore, relying solely on a trusted server is insufficient to resolve these privacy issues, as numerous server-targeted attacks have recently emerged. Exploiting the instruction-following capabilities of LMs, Qi et al. (2024) constructed context-based prompt attacks that can easily induce data leakage . Similarly, Zeng et al. (2024) formulated customized attack prompts tailored to specific types of extracted information, successfully executing both targeted and untargeted attacks against private data. Subsequently, several techniques have been proposed to mitigate privacy risks, including post-processing methods like reranking and summarization (Chase (2022)), but studies have indicated that these techniques cannot completely eliminate privacy risks (Zeng et al. (2024)). The inadequacy of these post-processing defenses in thwarting such attacks demonstrates the inherent vulnerability of storing raw data, highlighting the critical need for data-level privacy protection mechanisms.

2.2 Existing Protection Strategies for Knowledge Database Texts

Currently, researchers have conducted preliminary explorations into the privacy protection of knowledge database texts, which can be categorized into synthesis-based methods utilizing LLM text generation capabilities and perturbation-based methods based on differential privacy. In terms of data synthesis, focusing on privacy concerns, Tang et al. (2023) proposed a few-shot data generation method to produce private in-context demonstrations from private datasets . Furthermore, Zeng et al. (2025) pioneered the implementation of data synthesis based on the contextual information of original data in the field of privacy protection for knowledge database texts; they extracted a small amount of information from the original data to assist large models in data synthesis, and ensured that the text did not leak privacy through adversarial privacy evaluation LLMs. However, these methods overlook the sheer scale of text within knowledge databases. Relying on LLMs for such extensive generation tasks not only incurs prohibitive costs but also leads to significant information loss and increased hallucination rates.

To address these problems, researchers have shifted towards perturbation-based schemes. Differential Privacy (DP) (Dwork et al. (2006)) provides privacy guarantees for each record in a dataset by adding extra noise to query results to limit the impact of individual records; Feyisetan et al. (2020) employed a word-level perturbation method based on word embeddings for differential privacy perturbation, while Igamberdiev and Habernal (2023) proposed a sentence-level perturbation method based on paraphrase task language models from the perspective of semantic differences. Targeting the privacy protection of knowledge database texts, He et al. (2025) shifted their focus from the entire text to private entities, perturbing these private entities through a local differential privacy method that relies more heavily on the original text. However, for knowledge database texts requiring high accuracy to ensure the quality of LLM generation, such differential privacy methods suffer from uncertain entity perturbation, which degrades text readability. Furthermore, current studies universally lack privacy difference evaluation, making the intensity of entity perturbation unsuitable for privacy protection scenarios requiring differentiated protection levels. They all share the limitation of conflating text privacy protection with the privacy protection of scope entities, failing to properly define what constitutes text-level privacy protection in their problem formulation, which consequently causes a massive loss in utility.

3 Problem Formulation

3.1 Problem Definition

Recalling the example in Section 1, existing research on privacy protection for knowledge databases mostly remains at the stage of “scoped entity privacy protection”, which assumes that the privacy risk of a text is equivalent to the linear superposition of the privacy risks from individual, isolated sensitive entities. However, in the field of natural language processing, text is a continuous representation entity located in a high-dimensional semantic space. The privacy leakage risk of text primarily originates from the combinatorial inference risks generated by the intertwining of context, which shares a non-linear relationship with sensitive entities; when certain sensitive entities are anonymized, the semantic privacy risk of the text can be eliminated. Therefore, we posit that semantic privacy protection at the text level should not be the anonymization of all private entities, but rather maximizing the overall utility of the text through local anonymization while severing the semantic reconstruction paths.

To better quantify this concept, we model the text-level anonymization process of knowledge databases as a combinatorial optimization problem with privacy constraints. Given an original text TT in the knowledge database, assume its extractable entity set is E={e1,e2,…,en}E=\{e_{1},e_{2},\ldots,e_{n}\}. Let Φ\Phi be the entity anonymization function; our objective is to find an optimal subset of entities to be anonymized, denoted as EG⊆EE_{G}\subseteq E. We define a Boolean decision variable xe∈{0,1}x_{e}\in\{0,1\}, where xe=0x_{e}=0 indicates that the entity e∈EGe\in E_{G}, and xe=1x_{e}=1 indicates that the entity e∈E∖EGe\in E\setminus E_{G}. The contribution degree u⁡(e)u\left(e\right) of a single entity ee to the overall text utility can be formalized as the weighted sum of its normalized topical relevance and knowledge divergence:

u⁡(e)=β⋅Sr​e​t​r​(e)+γ⋅Sk​n​w​(e),u\left(e\right)=\beta\cdot S_{retr}\left(e\right)+\gamma\cdot S_{knw}\left(e\right), (1)

where β,γ>0\beta,\gamma>0 are hyperparameters adjusting the retrieval and knowledge weights. Consequently, the overall utility function 𝒰⁡(T,T′)\mathcal{U}\left(T,T^{\prime}\right) at the text level is defined as the sum of the utility contributions of all non-anonymized entities:

𝒰⁡(T,T′)=∑e∈Exe⋅u⁡(e),\mathcal{U}\left(T,T^{\prime}\right)=\sum_{e\in E}\ x_{e}\cdot u\left(e\right), (2)

Combining the aforementioned utility function, we can transform text semantic privacy protection into a constrained Boolean non-linear programming problem. To ensure that the privacy risk is within a controllable range, the text needs to satisfy semantic security and non-reconstructability. Finding the optimal generalized entity subset EG∗E_{G}^{*} that satisfies the above constraints to maximize 𝒰⁡(T,T′)\mathcal{U}\left(T,T^{\prime}\right) is an NP-Hard problem (the specific proof can be found in Appendix A). Therefore, this paper adopts a heuristic score mapping mechanism based on a greedy strategy to determine the anonymized entity subset (see Section 4).

3.2 Threat Model

We define the attacker 𝒜\mathcal{A} as an entity with polynomial-time computational capabilities. In the untrusted server scenario, 𝒜\mathcal{A} possesses white-box access privileges to the knowledge database; in the trusted server scenario, 𝒜\mathcal{A} possesses black-box access privileges to the RAG system and holds white-box knowledge regarding the anonymization mechanism Π\Pi. Since the individuals to which the texts in the knowledge database may refer possess the characteristic of being uncountable, the observation target of both types of attackers can be practically defined as a single generalized text. Furthermore, since data in sensitive domains is hard to obtain, attackers cannot actually gain background knowledge in the same way as they can with ordinary data.

The objectives of the attacker include: (1) Entity inference: recovering specific sensitive entities from the generalized text; (2) Document reconstruction: reconstructing the original document through combinatorial attacks utilizing residual information.(Goldwasser and Micali (2019))

4 Methods

4.1 Design and Workflow of TRIP-RAG

To overcome the inherent limitations of the "one-size-fits-all" text perturbation paradigm, we formalize the anonymization mechanism of knowledge databases as a constrained combinatorial optimization problem. The core intuition of TRIP-RAG is that different entities within a document possess heterogeneous impacts on semantic privacy risks and downstream task utility. As illustrated in Figure 2, our framework addresses this problem through a two-stage pipeline: (1) context-aware entity quantification, which evaluates the marginal contribution of each entity across privacy and utility dimensions; (2) dynamic generalization, which selectively anonymizes high-risk entities based on a greedy strategy while preserving the latent topological structure of the retrieval space and document knowledge.

4.1.1 Context-Aware Entity Quantification Phase

Let 𝒯\mathcal{T} denote the high-dimensional textual semantic space. Given an original document T∈𝒯T\in\mathcal{T} from an external knowledge base, we first deploy a bidirectional Transformer-based Named Entity Recognizer (NER), denoted as ℱN​E​R\mathcal{F}_{NER} (Zaratiana et al. (2024)), to extract the set of key entities E={e1,e2,…,en}E=\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{n}\}. Our objective is not to perform blind and arbitrary perturbation on EE, but rather to quantify the intrinsic trade-off for each entity e∈Ee\in E. We map this evaluation into a three-dimensional continuous manifold comprising marginal privacy risk, knowledge divergence, and topical relevance. Experimental verification shows that the information overlap rate of the scores in these three dimensions is very low. For specific details, see the Appendix B.

Marginal Privacy Risk (Sp​r​i​vS_{priv}). Text privacy is highly context-dependent, making isolated entity evaluation often suboptimal. To mathematically capture the contextual privacy leakage induced by a specific entity, we define a local anonymization operator Πe​(T)\Pi_{e}(T) to mask the entity ee within the text TT. Let fp​r​i​v:𝒯→ℝf_{priv}:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R} be a privacy-aware surrogate function parameterized by a pre-trained language model, which maps the document to its absolute privacy risk score (empirically calibrated via GDPR guidelines and compared with human evaluation via correlation coefficient analysis; see Appendix C). The privacy importance of entity ee is formally defined as its marginal contribution to the global contextual privacy risk:

Sp​r​i​v​(e)=fp​r​i​v​(T)−fp​r​i​v​(Πe​(T)),S_{priv}(e)=f_{priv}(T)-f_{priv}(\Pi_{e}(T)), (3)

This differential formulation directly quantifies the gradient of privacy leakage when a single entity is decoupled from the global semantics, thereby enabling scalable and context-aligned risk annotation.

Knowledge Divergence (Sk​n​wS_{knw}). To prevent severe information loss, we must preserve the entities that dominate the core knowledge of the document. Therefore, based on the semantic clustering hypothesis (Mikolov et al. (2013)), the removal of key entities may cause a catastrophic shift in the embedding space, which subsequently degrades knowledge utility. We introduce a pre-trained embedding encoder ℰ:𝒯→ℝd\mathcal{E}:\mathcal{T}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{d}. For a document TT and its perturbed version Πe​(T)\Pi_{e}(T), let 𝐡T=ℰ⁡(T)\mathbf{h}_{T}=\mathcal{E}(T) and 𝐡Πe​(T)=ℰ⁡(Πe​(T))\mathbf{h}_{\Pi_{e}(T)}=\mathcal{E}(\Pi_{e}(T)) denote their respective latent representations. We quantify this knowledge divergence by evaluating the cosine distance between them:

Sk​n​w​(e)=ℱn​o​r​m​(1−ℰ⁡(T)⋅ℰ⁡(Πe​(T))‖ℰ⁡(T)‖2||ℰ⁡(Πe​(T))||2),S_{knw}(e)=\mathcal{F}_{norm}\left(1-\frac{\mathcal{E}(T)\cdot\mathcal{E}(\Pi_{e}(T))}{||\mathcal{E}(T)||_{2}||\mathcal{E}(\Pi_{e}(T))||_{2}}\right),

 (4)

where ℱ′n​o​r​m​(⋅)\mathcal{F^{\prime}}_{norm}(\cdot) represents a robust normalization function. A larger angular shift signifies a higher contribution of the entity to the overall knowledge structure.

Topical Relevance (Sr​e​t​rS_{retr}). RAG systems inherently rely on vector space geometry to conduct similarity search (Lewis et al. (2020)). For the document TT and the entity ee, let 𝐡T=ℰ⁡(T)\mathbf{h}_{T}=\mathcal{E}(T) and 𝐡e=ℰ⁡(e)\mathbf{h}_{e}=\mathcal{E}(e) denote their latent representations, respectively. We utilize the entity to simulate a retrieval query, thereby measuring the L2L_{2} divergence between the entity topic and the global document topic to quantify the topic relevance of ee to the document:

Sr​e​t​r​(e)=ℱn​o​r​m​(−‖𝐡e−𝐡T‖2),S_{retr}(e)=\mathcal{F}_{norm}(-||\mathbf{h}_{e}-\mathbf{h}_{T}||_{2}), (5)

A smaller divergence indicates that the entity is more relevant to the retrieval of the document.

4.1.2 Dynamic Generalization Phase

In the second phase, the framework identifies the optimal subset of entities to be anonymized by solving a surrogate optimization objective. We aggregate the three decoupled dimensions mentioned above into a unified entity priority score Ψ⁡(e)\Psi(e), parameterized by weighting coefficients α,β,γ≥0\alpha,\beta,\gamma\geq 0:

Ψ⁡(e)=α​Sp​r​i​v​(e)−β​Sr​e​t​r​(e)−γ​Sk​n​w​(e),\Psi(e)=\alpha S_{priv}(e)-\beta S_{retr}(e)-\gamma S_{knw}(e), (6)

This formulation balances the objective of maximizing the reduction of privacy risks (driven by Sp​r​i​vS_{priv}) against the penalties of utility degradation (constrained by Sr​e​t​rS_{retr} and Sk​n​wS_{knw}).

Dynamic Threshold Determination. Given that different vertical domains (e.g., healthcare and financial services) exhibit extreme heterogeneity in privacy sensitivity distributions, traditional static Top-K truncation strategies are highly susceptible to destroying the topological structure of the high-dimensional semantic space, thereby leading to suboptimal solutions with over-anonymization. Recalling the problem formulation in Section 3.1, since semantic privacy possesses strong context dependence, we introduce a Large Language Model (LLM) as an evaluator. By executing a single-turn dialogue on a small number of samples, we can extract the critical subset of entities necessary to eliminate semantic privacy risks. By comparing the Ψ⁡(e)\Psi(e) scores of these entities, we can empirically determine a safe critical threshold τ\tau. Specifically, we bound the subset EGE_{G} of entities to be anonymized based on the obtained empirical threshold, incorporating entities with scores exceeding the threshold into this set. We additionally conducted a manual secondary evaluation of the LLM’s assessment results; detailed settings can be found in Appendix D:

EG={e∈E∣Ψ⁡(e)>τ},E_{G}=\{e\in E\mid\Psi(e)>\tau\}, (7)

Semantics-Preserving Entity Anonymization. To ensure that the perturbed document T′T^{\prime} can maintain the strict syntactic coherence and factual consistency required for downstream LLM reasoning, we discard destructive operations such as token dropping. Instead, we define a secure generalization mapping ℳ:ℒ→𝒟\mathcal{M}:\mathcal{L}\rightarrow\mathcal{D}, which projects the original semantic label le∈ℒl_{e}\in\mathcal{L} of entity ee into a safe, coarse-grained descriptor space 𝒟\mathcal{D} (Specific generalization mapping tables and replacement examples can be found in Appendix E). The system iteratively applies the transformation Γ⁡(e)=ℳ⁡(le)\Gamma(e)=\mathcal{M}(l_{e}) to all e∈EGe\in E_{G}. At this point, TRIP-RAG successfully neutralizes exact sensitive attributes while strictly preserving the structure and semantic topology of the external knowledge base.

4.2 Security Analysis

Given the attacker’s objectives outlined in Section 3.2, we need to analyze the semantic security and non-reconstructability of the proposed method.

4.2.1 Proof of Semantic Security

If, after observing the anonymized text T′=Π⁡(T)T^{\prime}=\Pi(T), the advantage of an attacker in distinguishing between any two original entities e0,e1e_{0},e_{1} belonging to the same generalization class CC is negligible, i.e.,

Adv𝒜s​e​m(λ)=|Pr[𝒜(Π(Te0))=1]−Pr[𝒜(Π(Te1))=1]|≤ϵ(λ),Adv_{\mathcal{A}}^{sem}\left(\lambda\right)=\left|Pr\left[\mathcal{A}\left(\Pi\left(T_{e_{0}}\right)\right)=1\right]-Pr\left[\mathcal{A}\left(\Pi\left(T_{e_{1}}\right)\right)=1\right]\right|\leq\epsilon\left(\lambda\right),

 (8)

then the mechanism Π\Pi is said to satisfy semantic security. It is easy to see that the generalization function Φ\Phi is a non-injective surjection. Furthermore, since the objects being generalized, such as names, are highly extensive, the pre-image cardinality |Φ−1​(c)|\left|\Phi^{-1}\left(c\right)\right| of the generalization class is sufficiently large. Therefore, the entity generalization mechanism of TRIP-RAG achieves semantic indistinguishability against an attacker in polynomial time, i.e., A​d​v𝒜s​e​m≈0Adv_{\mathcal{A}}^{sem}\approx 0. The detailed proof can be found in Appendix F.1.

4.2.2 Proof of Non-reconstructability

For a given anonymized text T′T^{\prime}, if the residual Shannon entropy of the original text TT satisfies H⁡(T|T′)≥ηH(T|T^{\prime})\geq\eta, then the system is said to satisfy non-reconstructability. Based on the dynamic threshold mechanism, TRIP-RAG can ensure that all high-specificity entities are partitioned into the generalization set EGE_{G} by adjusting the threshold. Against any polynomial-time reconstruction attack, the system guarantees that the upper bound of the document reconstruction probability is 2−η2^{-\eta}, thus satisfying non-reconstructability. The detailed proof can be found in Appendix F.2.

5 Experiment

In this section, we demonstrate through cross-dataset and multi-model experiments that our proposed scheme effectively quantifies and balances privacy and utility. First, we introduce the experimental setup in Section 5.1, encompassing dataset and model selection, baseline models, evaluation metrics, and implementation details. Subsequently, we present the results regarding utility and privacy protection in Section 5.2. Finally, we conduct ablation studies in Section 5.3 to demonstrate the necessity of each constituent module within our architecture, as well as to validate the rationale behind our hyperparameter settings and training sample sizes.

5.1 Experimental Setup

Datasets and Models. For privacy protection scenarios, we adopted the ChatDoctor-HealthCareMagic-100k dataset utilized by He et al. (2025), which encompasses over 100,000 doctor-patient conversations containing extensive personal information such as names and ages. Based on scenario requirements, we selected the Enronqa dataset provided by Ryan et al. (2025). This dataset was derived from the Enron emails corpus through filtering operations to obtain 70,000 authentic workplace Q&A pairs, which include personal information such as names and private phone numbers. Thereby validating our method’s effectiveness in two representative sensitive domains: healthcare and business. Following the evaluation protocols of the baseline methods, we allocated 99% of the dataset for retrieval purposes and the remaining 1% for testing. We selected Llama2-7b-chat (Touvron et al. (2023)) as the LLM for performance evaluation, and utilized the Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B model (Zhang et al. (2025)) , the bge-large-en-v1.5 model (Xiao et al. (2024)) alongside the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 model as the embedding models.

Baselines. To verify the effectiveness of our method, we incorporated three baselines, including full generalized mapping replacement, paraphrasing methods, and a representative existing knowledge database anonymization method—namely, the anonymization method based on local differential privacy proposed by He et al. (2025). Detailed information regarding these methods is provided in Appendix G. Additionally, we included the results from the original data for comparison.

Metrics. We employ three categories of metrics to evaluate post-anonymization retrieval performance, utility, and privacy protection. For retrieval performance, referring to the study by Thakur et al. (2021), we incorporated Recall@k as the evaluation metric to illustrate the post-anonymization divergence from the original knowledge. For utility evaluation, we utilized the following metrics: ROUGE-L (Lin (2004)) to measure the accuracy and overlap between the original text and the reconstructed text, and the BLEU score (Papineni et al. (2002)) to assess the n-gram similarity between the two. For privacy protection, following the privacy evaluation methodology of He et al. (2025), we adopted the privacy extraction attack proposed by Zeng et al. (2024) to measure the method’s resistance against contextual inference capabilities. This attack extracts relevant retrieved documents by formulating “information + command” prompts. It quantifies the privacy protection of each baseline by counting the privacy entities present in the LLM-generated text.

Implementations. Both the storage of embeddings and the construction of the retrieval database were implemented using the FAISS library. By default, we employed L2L_{2}-norm as the distance metric to compare embeddings. In experiments outside the scope of exploring retrieval performance, we uniformly retrieved 5 documents to serve as the Context. For entity extraction and the batch scoring of privacy importance scores, we utilized the gliner-v2.1 model (Zaratiana et al. (2024)) and the deberta-v3-base model (He et al. (2021)), respectively. For α\alpha, β\beta, and γ\gamma, we assigned the values of 1, 0.5, and 0.4, respectively, and following the dynamic threshold determination mechanism outlined in Section 4.1.2, we established the threshold for ChatDoctor-HealthCareMagic-100k at 0.6237, and the threshold for Enronqa at 0.564 . All experimental evaluations were executed on an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU.

5.2 Main Results

We conducted extensive experiments across multiple datasets and models to evaluate retrieval performance, answer utility, and security. The experimental results further demonstrate the superiority and advancement of our framework.

5.2.1 Utility Evaluation

To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we report the ROUGE-L and BLEU scores between the generated answers and the ground truth to assess the quality of the generated responses. Furthermore, to demonstrate the information retention of our method, we additionally incorporated Recall@k, illustrating the degree of variance from the original knowledge post-anonymization by comparing the overlap of retrieval results between the original documents and the anonymized documents under identical queries.

The results, as shown in Table 1, indicate that our method maintains superior information integrity compared to the baseline methods, fully proving that we preserve the actual utility of the original data. Compared to paraphrasing methods such as Paraphrase, we adhere to and retain the original knowledge more closely, achieving the best scores on the Recall@k metric with an improvement of 9%-60% over the baseline methods. Compared to comprehensive anonymization methods like LPRAG that neglect differentiation and holism in privacy protection, we obtained the optimal scores on the BLEU and ROUGE-L metrics through the study of entity differentiation, improving BLEU by 3%-56% and ROUGE-L by 5%-53% relative to the baseline methods.

5.2.2 Privacy Protection Analysis

We employ the privacy extraction attack proposed by Zeng et al. (2024). After being processed by the anonymization method, the documents should not expose sensitive entities when answering questions; if sensitive entities are exposed, it indicates that the LLM has achieved contextual re-identification of the sensitive entities.

As shown in Table 2, we achieve the best results on the ChatDoctor dataset, reducing privacy leakage by 26% compared to the original data. On the Enronqa dataset, we reduce privacy leakage by 48% compared to the original data. Although the Paraphrase method is slightly superior to ours in terms of privacy protection, as can be seen from Table 1, it loses too much information. While its private information is reduced, its utility becomes almost unusable, whereas our method can still maintain the highest utility, demonstrating the superiority of our approach.

5.3 Ablation Study

We conducted three ablation studies on TRIP-RAG to evaluate the rationality of the framework design and hyperparameter selection. We utilized the all-MiniLM-L6-v2 as the embedding model and evaluated our method on the ChatDoctor dataset.

Dimensional Ablation. Given the necessity of privacy protection, we investigate the advantages of incorporating topic relevance and knowledge divergence into the framework. As shown in Table 3, compared to the model based solely on marginal privacy risk, the inclusion of topical relevance yields improvements of 16% and 15% in the retrieval metrics Recall@1 and Recall@5. Similarly, incorporating knowledge divergence leads to a 10% improvement in the utility metric BLEU-1 compared to the privacy-risk-only model. The full model achieves overall improvements of 23%, 18%, and 12% in Recall@1, Recall@5, and BLEU-1, respectively.

Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis. We fix α=1\alpha=1 as the anchor, and assign values of 0.2, 0.4, 0.5, 0.6, 0.8, and 1.0 to the weights β\beta and γ\gamma, respectively, to obtain the heatmap of the retrieval metric Recall@1 and the bar chart of the utility metric BLEU and ROUGE-L. It can be observed that as β\beta and γ\gamma increase, the retrieval metrics exhibit a favorable synchronous upward trend. The Spearman correlation coefficient between wr+wkw_{r}+w_{k} and Recall@5 is 0.8561 (p-value < 0.0001), indicating a significant and strong positive correlation. Regarding the answer quality, it is straightforward to understand that it is jointly influenced by the retrieval results and the contained knowledge; therefore, we aim to obtain an optimal hyperparameter ratio to maximize the answer quality. As shown in the Figure 3, we select two ratios to present in the text. Based on the average value of the BLEU metric, we select γ:β=0.8\gamma:\beta=0.8 as the optimal ratio.

Impact of Labeled Data on Privacy Scoring. We selected sample sizes of 2, 4, 6, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, and 200 for training, and calculated the Spearman correlation coefficient against manually annotated test samples. The results, as illustrated in the Figure 3, demonstrate that as the number of samples increases, the model’s scoring progressively aligns with human judgment standards. At a sample size of 128, a strong positive correlation of nearly 0.8 is achieved. With the 200 samples utilized in this study, the correlation coefficient reaches 0.9160, indicating that the model is fundamentally consistent with human judgment.

6 Conclusions

We highlight the distinction between text semantic-level privacy protection and scope-entity privacy protection, correcting the misconceptions regarding text semantic privacy protection from the perspective of problem formulation. We focus on the variability of privacy protection intensity and the disparities among entities, constructing a dynamic anonymization framework tailored for knowledge databases by defining the marginal privacy risk, knowledge divergence, and topical relevance of entities. Through cross-dataset and multi-model experiments, we demonstrate that our proposed scheme quantifies and balances privacy and utility, achieving a percentage improvement in utility while having almost no impact on privacy. The evaluation framework proposed in this paper can also be extended to the broader field of text anonymization and integrated with various downstream anonymization methods, providing a novel reference and a controllable-intensity perspective for text semantic privacy protection.

7 Limitation

In this study, we rely on the GLiNER model to extract private entities (Zaratiana et al. (2024)) for the experimental portion of the paper. Although our investigation indicates that this custom-label-based extraction method is currently the state-of-the-art and the most suitable approach for privacy protection scenarios, our manual audit of the extraction results reveals that this method still misses some entities that appear in uncommon positions. Nevertheless, our overall experimental and evaluation results are based exclusively on the identified entity content, which does not compromise the experimental findings of this paper, but we look forward to future breakthroughs in entity extraction research.

Appendix A Reduction of the Problem of Finding the Optimal Generalized Entity Subset

We prove this by performing a polynomial-time reduction from the classical 0-1 knapsack problem to our anonymization optimization problem. Consider a special case scenario where the background knowledge of the attacker faced by the system is extremely scarce, such that the generalization of any single entity is sufficient to satisfy the anti-reconstruction entropy constraint η\eta. Under this special case, non-reconstructability becomes a non-binding constraint and can be ignored. At this point, the optimization problem degenerates into: selecting a subset of entities XX subject to a total capacity limit, such that the total “value” ueu_{e} of these entities is maximized. In this mapping: the entity’s privacy Sp​r​i​veS_{priv}^{e} is equivalent to the weight of an item in the knapsack problem; the entity’s utility contribution ueu_{e} is equivalent to the value of an item in the knapsack problem; and the privacy threshold Bp​r​i​vB_{priv} is equivalent to the maximum capacity of the knapsack. Since the 0-1 knapsack problem is universally recognized as an NP-Hard problem in the classical combinatorial optimization field, and the aforementioned special case is merely a proper subset of the problem proposed in this paper, the original problem is at least as hard as the 0-1 knapsack problem. Namely, this problem is strongly NP-Hard.

Appendix B Information Overlap Among the Three Features

We employ the Spearman correlation coefficient to investigate whether there is an information overlap among the three features. As demonstrated in the Table 4, the maximum correlation coefficient is merely 0.4166. By calculating the square of the correlation coefficients to estimate the proportion of their shared rank variance, it can be observed that at least 80% of the information remains independent. Appendix C Privacy Annotation Details

C.1 Data Sampling and Annotation Guidelines

To construct a high-quality training dataset for privacy scores, we adopted a random sampling method. We randomly sampled 200 representative text snippets rich in entities from the dataset, respectively. We recruited two researchers with backgrounds in Natural Language Processing (NLP) and foundational knowledge in data privacy protection to serve as independent annotators. Prior to formal annotation, all annotators underwent specialized training focused on the core privacy definitions of the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) to ensure consistency in annotation standards.

The specific regulation content we referred to is as follows:

‘personal data’ means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person (‘data subject’); an identifiable natural person is one who can be identified, directly or indirectly, in particular by reference to an identifier such as a name, an identification number, location data, an online identifier or to one or more factors specific to the physical, physiological, genetic, mental, economic, cultural or social identity of that natural person;

We established the following 4-level scoring rubric to quantify the privacy importance score of entities:

  • •

    Level 3 (Score 0.7-1.0): Entities that can directly and uniquely pinpoint a specific individual. Examples: real names, identification numbers, telephone numbers, exact home addresses, etc.

  • •

    Level 2 (Score 0.4-0.7): Entities posing moderate isolated risks but potential inference risks in context, or personal information susceptible to temporal factors.Examples: real age, biometric characteristics.

  • •

    Level 1 (Score 0.1-0.4): Entities that contain certain personal characteristics but possess a high degree of generalization within a large population, or entities for which auxiliary inference information is difficult to obtain. Examples: broad geographical regions (e.g., California), medical diagnostic results, and major business decisions.

  • •

    Level 0 (Score 0.0-0.1): General vocabulary or objective medical/business terminology that essentially does not involve personal privacy. Examples: common drug names (e.g., insulin), common symptoms, and general corporate operations.

C.2 Comparison Between Language Model and Human Evaluation

To validate the reliability of the language model’s privacy risk evaluation, we conducted a correlation analysis between the model’s assigned scores and the human annotations. We utilized the Spearman correlation coefficient to measure the monotonic relationship between the two sets of evaluations. The analysis demonstrated a highly strong alignment, achieving a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.91390.9139 on the ChatDoctor dataset and 0.90850.9085 on the Enronqa dataset. These results indicate that the privacy-aware surrogate function’s evaluations are fundamentally consistent with human judgment standards.

Appendix D Threshold Determination Details

We designed the following single-turn dialogue prompt for the LLM to guide it to focus on the combinatorial inference risks arising from intertwined contexts, rather than viewing entities in isolation:

To validate the reliability of our approach, we additionally recruited two researchers specializing in Natural Language Processing (NLP) to conduct a manual secondary evaluation of the LLM-assessed samples. The results reveal that the entity subsets extracted by the LLM strictly subsume those identified by human evaluators. Although the LLM occasionally extracts redundant entities—leading to a generally lower overall score—anonymizing supplementary entities introduces no additional privacy compromises. Furthermore, the downstream utility still maintains a clear advantage over naive baselines that anonymize all recognized entities. Therefore, we conclude that adopting the LLM-based evaluation paradigm is sound.

F.2 Proof of Non-reconstructability

We model the reconstruction attack as an attempt to minimize the conditional entropy H⁡(T|T′)H\left({T}\middle|T^{\prime}\right). Let EG={e∈E|Ψ⁡(e)≥τ}E_{G}\ =\ \{e\ \in E\ |\ \Psi(e)\ \geq\tau\} be the set of generalized entities. The dynamic threshold τ\tau ensures that entities with high privacy scores or high information content are included in EGE_{G}.For an attacker to reconstruct T, they must correctly guess the pre-image for every generalized slot. Let Δc\Delta_{c} be the size of the plausible candidate set for a label c. The probability of exact reconstruction is bounded by:

Appendix G Introduction to Experimental Baseline Methods

  • •

    Redact obtains the anonymized text by performing a generalized mapping replacement on the identified and extracted entities based on their labels.

  • •

    Paraphrase utilizes the capabilities of LLMs to extract relevant and important components from the retrieved context. Less important parts can be filtered out, and certain sentences may require rewriting. The prompt we used for paraphrasing is shown in Prompt G.

  • •

    LPRAG The LPRAG method employs three modules—a word perturbation module, a phrase perturbation module, and a number perturbation module—to perform local differential privacy perturbation. During our reproduction, we allocated a global privacy budget of 5.0.
